This council, which is to consider our industrial and financial development and present proposals in a united way for the first time, has a motto which expresses the hope that the maritimes will be a better part of a better Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have spoken in the house since I was elected in 1953. I understand it is customary for members making their first speech to deal with matters pertaining specifically to their own constituencies. I want to talk about several phases of our economy in Prince Edward Island and tell you something about the excellent standards we have achieved in our primary products. I also want to say to the house that, although we are small in size, we have achieved top rank in the production of some of the very best products of this great country.
Before I go into that, may I make a general observation. I have noted with some concern a tendency toward sectionalism on the part of some in this chamber in their approach to problems that affect all of us as Canadians. I call this a great country, but how can it be great unless we, as elected representatives of the people, are broadminded enough to have the interests of all the people at heart?
I know that the problems of my province do not directly affect many people in other parts of Canada. You have problems that do not affect my people, but all these problems affect the economy of Canada. Therefore, to that extent at least, I think all of us should have mutual interests. For example, I hear spokesmen for farm groups saying the farmers are not getting a fair deal and their rightful share of the national income. They protest that we do not appreciate the position of the farmer, his value in the national economy and his worth. I use the farm spokesmen merely as an example. I could have referred to any one of a number of other groups.
I am going to tell you something about the farming achievements of Prince Edward Island, but before I do so may I suggest that if some hon. members do not appreciate the farmers' problems it may well be the fault of those members who are the spokesmen for areas where farming is the dominant factor. It may be we have failed to explain


the farmers' position and paint a true picture of his worth. We know that Canada needs a strong and growing agricultural economy, but have we made our urban friends aware of that fact?
Nobody is more conscious of some of the agricultural problems than I am. I know that many city folk fail to realize these problems. But I am not going to try to win the support of my urban friends by kicking them in the shins. I am not going to try to win their friendship and understanding by antagonizing them. I do not believe in carrying a chip on my shoulder when I am trying to sell my ideas to others.
May I, therefore, make this observation directed specifically to people in the city areas. Do not forget that you need the farmer. What would you and your families eat if he did not grow the foodstuffs that stock your great supermarkets? Do not forget that he often produces this food at a loss, or at a price that does not give him a working profit. Remember also that in producing the food he has to sell it at the price that somebody else wants to pay. Imagine a lawyer taking what his client wants to pay instead of the set fee which he demands and gets as his right. Imagine a merchant selling groceries, or clothing, or hardware or any other commodity for what the customer wanted to pay.
Before some of my city friends start throwing missiles at me, let me add that the farmer needs the city people just as much as they need him. If it were not for our great metropolitan centres, our smaller cities and towns, where would the farmer sell his products? I am not a farmer. I am a newspaperman, but I do own a small farm and live in the country. In that way I have kept closely in touch with the problems of the farmer.
If I may digress for a moment, I may say that for ten years I sat in the press gallery of our provincial legislature. I would feel much more at home in the press gallery here now than I do making my first speech in this chamber.
I speak of agricultural problems first because agriculture is the dominant factor in our provincial economy. My riding includes Charlottetown, our capital city and our largest centre. Therefore a large portion of my constituents are urban people. I have lived and worked among them for many years. But because we have no industries, as most of you understand the term, we depend for the most part on agriculture. We also have our fishing industry and our tourist business. Both of them are very important. I am not unmindful of the problems of city people

because I have lived and worked among them for 20 years. In fact recently at home I have been in closer touch with urban groups than I have been with the farm people, and I have tried to keep in close touch with them throughout the years.
One problem causing concern in our area now is the potato trade between our country and the United States. As many of you probably know, we work on a quota basis. We are allowed to ship into the United States-I say "we" but it is mostly New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island that fill the quota-2-5 million bushels of seed potatoes and 1 million bushels as table stock. There is a rider to the agreement, which is based on the total volume of the United States crop, which sometimes gives us the opportunity of shipping an extra amount of table stock. But even under the quota we pay a duty of 37-5 cents per hundred pounds, and for amounts above the quota we pay 75 cents per hundred pounds.
Some years ago the United States was given permission to ship potatoes into our country duty free. There is one exception which I should mention, and I believe that refers to about one month during the summer when protection is afforded to the growers in the southern Ontario peninsula. With that one exception I do not think United States shippers pay any duty at all on potatoes shipped into this country.
A few months ago potatoes were rolling across the border from Maine in such a volume that both growers and shippers in my province and New Brunswick viewed the problem with grave concern. The matter was brought to the attention of the responsible people here, and I was glad to hear the Minister of Finance say in his budget speech that it will be turned over to the tariff board for their consideration. I know that tariffs are a difficult and complicated problem, but I hope the board can find some solution for our particular difficulty.
The potato situation at home right now is good. Some two or three weeks ago the price soared to $3.20 a bushel, that is the price to the farmer. It is somewhat less now, but it is still good. However, sudden price fluctuations are bad for any industry. The potato industry is no exception. At their peak they cause terrifically high prices to the consumer, and therefore discourage consumption. They are often likely to cause very heavy planting the following year. The results are sometimes chaotic and at times even disastrous.
But potato growing is only one phase of our farming program. I want to tell you 50433-205
The Budget-Mr. Matheson something about our Yorkshire hogs. We have developed a special bacon type. The Canadian Press had a story last week concerning a new type of bacon hog that is being developed at the experimental farm at Lacombe, Alberta. The story says, in part, that they aim at faster maturing animals with more vigour. The dams are good mothers, the story says. The young pigs are bigger. It sounds like the sort of thing we have been developing for 30 years in our island Yorkshires. This is a big statement to make, but I am going to make it. We have the best bacon hog in this country. Here is the proof. It is from an official publication, and if anyone wants to check it, it is the Livestock Market Review, published by the marketing information section of the marketing service, Department of Agriculture, Ottawa, Canada.
This information appears on page 87 and is given in some detail, but I have summarized it to save time. You will find that in 1953 our island breeders had 51-3 per cent grade A or the top grade it is possible to produce in bacon hogs. Nova Scotia had 43-1 per cent and New Brunswick 38-1 per cent. The others were far behind. Last year Prince Edward Island had 53-6 per cent. Alberta was lowest with 18-2 per cent. The results for the other three years were the same. Our province was well ahead. In 1951 we had 53-1 per cent in the top grade. No other province can touch our record in the production of top grade bacon hogs.
Here is further proof of the excellence of our island Yorkshires and the high value people in other provinces place on them. I am quoting from the Charlottetown newspaper, the Guardian, under date of April 22, 1955. The heading is "Demand exceeds supply for famed island Yorkshires". The article reads in part:
"In the face of recent shipments of Yorkshire breeding stock from this province and in view of the expected requirements, our island breeders are not going to be able to meet outside demand", said Mr. H. W. Clay, senior livestock field man, production branch, federal Department of Agriculture, yesterday.
Mr. Clay is quoting from a letter written by Mr. Longman, deputy minister of agriculture in Alberta, to Mr. Frank Baker, western director of the Canadian industrial council of meat packers. Mr. Baker was in touch with Mr. Clay and the letter states in part -this is Mr. Longman speaking-
The question is-how can we bring this about? Why is P.E.I. attaining the reputation it has with respect to hogs? .	.	. An examination of the
P.E.I. situation might be extremely profitable to the farmers of Alberta . . . Alberta hog producers must adopt the principles and practices which have brought about the improvement in P.E.I.

The Budget-Mr. Matheson
That is the end of the quotation from the letter, but the newspaper article continues:
Within recent weeks breeding stock, mostly boars, has gone to the following destinations throughout Canada:
I have listed a few of them. There are Dorchester penitentiary, Grand Falls, Hart-land, Harvey Station, and several other places in New Brunswick. There are Czar and Red Deer and Edmonton in Alberta. There are Dunnville, London, Bath, Chats-worth, Hawkestone and Brunner in Ontario. There is Gaspe in Quebec. Mr. Clay has stated that shipments outside the province over the same period of time have never been equalled. In addition to these, he says he is reasonably sure "that a party from Edmonton, Alberta, is coming back to the island in late May to purchase a carload, and only yesterday he received an inquiry from an Alberta farm organization regarding the possibility of procuring young boars". The demand has been so keen, according to Mr. Clay, that "there are practically no young boars available in the province".
This latter story concerns our registered, purebred swine and the demand that exists for them. The previous story concerns animals produced by our commercial breeders. Correlate the two stories and you have the answer to our hog supremacy in producing the type of bacon the discerning Canadian wants on his breakfast plate. The registered breeder of purebred swine furnishes the foundation stock for our top commercial herds. Our purebred swine are kept on a high level by the continuous testing that is done through the medium of advanced registry, under the careful direction of the Department of Agriculture. This is part of the service for which you and I, as Canadians, pay; but in our province we have made a little better use of it than they have elsewhere.
Let me illustrate. The term "carcass score" will not mean much to you unless you are familiar with it. The better the animal, the higher the score. It measures the prolificacy of the dam. It considers the liveability of the young. It measures the rate at which the litter reaches market weight. It checks the amount of feed required to produce a pound of bacon. It takes into account the type and quality of bacon that the test group produce when they go on the rail. The information is used to assess and evaluate the breeding qualities of the sire and the dam, the ability to pass on desirable qualities to their young. Desirable sires and dams are kept for breeding purposes, while the undesirable are destroyed.

It is as simple as the theory of natural selection, but in this case science and practical knowledge are used to speed up and intensify the selective process. I checked through official figures for 1952 and 1953, and I am quoting from a publication of the production service of the Canadian Department of Agriculture. Anyone who is interested can check what I am saying. I checked through the figures for 1952 and 1953. Last year's figures are not immediately available.
In 1952, for example, I found that in the whole of Canada there were only 22 sires that sired litters with scores of 90 or more. A score of 90 is most unusual. Fifteen of the 22 were bred in my province. There were 18 dams with scores of 90 or more. Twelve of them were bred in Prince Edward Island. Of many hundreds of dams tested, only four in all Canada had a score of 95. All of them were from our province. The figures for 1953 are almost equally significant. One animal sired two test litters that scored 95. Our numbers naturally are much smaller than the combined numbers of the other provinces, but we have by far the most top scoring animals, both sires and dams. Our commercial herds carry the blood lines of those outstanding individuals of proven value. It is easy to understand why our bacon grades are so consistently high.
My constituency of Queens is not usually considered a producer of top grade beef cattle, though we do have some top flight animals. But our fat stock show and sale, held this year, brought an average price of 28 [DOT] 88 cents per pound on the hoof. That was the best in eastern Canada. I do not know whether you can beat that in western Canada. My neighbour, Athol Roberts, of Southport, is the president of the organization. All the championship animals in this outstanding show came from my constituency.
I am happy about a new development in our Atlantic provinces. This was referred to by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell). It is called the Atlantic provinces development council. It has the blessing of the four Atlantic premiers and their governments, but it is being administered, fostered and financed by industry. I spoke a few days ago to Keith MacKinnon in Charlottetown, our island vice-president of the council. Here is part of what he had to say:
The formation of the Atlantic provinces economic council symbolizes "self help" for maritime business, and the prospect of a new deal for the economic life of maritime citizens.
It symbolizes leadership by the businessmen themselves in appraising their own problems. Through the research and technical facilities available, the idea is to work toward improving the production, marketing, and utilization of goods and services of these provinces by the sea.

The Atlantic provinces have played an important part in the building of Canada. Canada grew westward, and with the development of its vast resources and industries-waterpower, manufacturing, transportation, minerals, oil, gas and pipelines, grain, lumber and livestock-the spotlight has turned away from maritime business.
However, our resources are not depleted. Agriculture, fisheries, minerals, lumber and the untapped natural facilities for a profitable tourist and holiday trade, leave us much with which to prosper.
With this new instrument at our disposal we can put our collective minds to work at the task of finding new ways and bettering old, in making the best use of our resources to bring about that new prosperity that is surely our due.
Our government has made a fine start in economic development in my province. Premier A. W. Matheson and his government will be calling an election very soon. Their return is assured. They have the confidence of the people as no other administration has had for some time. They have earned that confidence.
Earlier this year Premier Matheson announced a program of industrial development designed to assist fishing and agriculture. It will also assist the urban people by providing employment. The government set up a fund to assist such development. Already one reasonably large processing plant is being organized. There is a possibility of a very large one coming into the province in the near future. Foods grown on the island will be processed on the island. This sort of thing could make a great difference; it could be a great boon to our economic development. For years they talked about rural electrification in our province. Premier Matheson set the plan in motion. I might say in passing that the premier is no relation of mine.
I have to strike one sour note at this stage. It concerns an important industry that was started two years ago in Charlottetown by two very fine young men. They produce Perfection brand condensed milk. It is a splendid product, which can compete in quality with any similar product produced anywhere. It has been doing that very successfully. Right now, however, the product is faced with a price-cutting campaign by a very large and very powerful company that has been selling condensed milk for many years.
The development of this plant has meant a good deal to our agriculture and to our economy in general. Further development of this local industry could mean even more. I do not know just how serious the threat t.o the Perfection people may be, but it is another example of how some of the big firms will try to squeeze out competition to maintain the monopoly they invariably seem so anxious to have.
50433-205J
The Budget-Mr. Matheson
I said that our fishing industry is important. Our lobster fishermen are now preparing for the opening of the 1955 season. Theirs is a difficult task. They are hardy and fearless men, these fishermen who brave the storms and the turbulent seas to wrest their living from the deep. They have come through many adversities. They have persevered in the face of discouragement and disaster. They deserve happier days. I am glad to note that there has been some improvement. New and modern processing plants make for a better product, and an increase in consumption should be the result.
I congratulate the Department of Fisheries upon the splendid advertising job they are doing through their fish kitchen in the west block. I recently attended a dinner there, at which my friend the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Fisheries was host. The meals they serve are attractive and delicious. If we could have fish served in our commercial eating establishments as it is served there we would have no worries about a market. We would eat our fish right here in our own country. Like all islanders I am very modest, but our island lobsters rank with the best anywhere in the world. The fame of our oysters has spread far and wide. We have other fish products that tempt the appetite of the discerning diner.
About a year ago I asked a question of my good friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters). It concerned the calling of tenders for a new federal building in Charlottetown. I remember the shouts of derision from across the way. They were good-natured shouts, but they indicated that nothing would be done. The minister indicated tenders would be called by the 1st of June. Work is progressing favourably, and the builders tell me the steel work will be completed the first week in May. I thank the minister and his departmental officials for their co-operation in several matters relating to this project. A modification of plans meant that work could proceed during the early months of the year, which meant employment for a number of people who otherwise would have been idle.
We talked for some time this session about unemployment. We talk of a "shelf of public works" to provide work. I shall welcome any work that is useful, but major projects do not provide nearly as much work now as they did in the past. Our federal building property covers half a city block. The site had to be cleared, and a huge excavation job was necessary. Before the development of today's power machinery it would have provided work for several hundred men for perhaps six months or more. The job was

The Budget-Mr. Matheson done in six weeks by a handful of men and some powerful machinery. This is a sample of modern efficiency, but I sometimes wonder just how far this development can go. One cannot make progress by turning back the hands of the clock, but the shimmering glimpses of future trends are sometimes cause for concern.
My thanks are due the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) and his officials for their very splendid co-operation in the planning of a new car ferry between Wood Island in my constituency and Caribou, Nova Scotia. I have also received the utmost co-operation and courtesy from the members of the Canadian maritime commission and those associated with them. The target for completion of the new boat is the season of 1956. I await with a great deal of anticipation the day when the new ferry will be able to handle the traffic that develops at both ends of the ferry run.
My thanks are due also to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who interrupted his vacation last summer to speak at the 100th anniversary celebration at St. Dunstan's University, just outside Charlottetown. I am glad the genial minister found restful relaxation and wonderful swimming for a few days on the silvery sands and in the stimulating salt water along the north shore of my riding.
I hope many of you will visit Charlottetown this year to participate in its centennial program. The committee in charge have prepared a splendid program of fun and entertainment. In their name I invite you to visit this year the city where Canada was born. It was there in 1864 that the first discussion on confederation was held. There in the very room where the delegates met more than 90 years ago you can see the table around which they sat. The very chairs have been kept through the years. In the old visitors' book you can see the handwriting of Sir John A. Macdonald, who indicated his occupation as a "cabinet maker". It is an exhilarating experience to stand in the confederation chamber and think that here the fathers of confederation held their first momentous meeting. Here the history of our country was shaped.
I have in my room official invitations from the mayor of Charlottetown asking you to visit our beautiful city this coming summer. I shall have them distributed to you in the near future. They are novel and interesting. I hope you will keep them as souvenirs; but I hope you will accept the invitation and come to see us.
A few weeks ago the Canadian Association of Radio and Television Broadcasters hon-


oured posthumously the late Colonel Keith Rogers. They conferred on him an honour given to pioneers of the radio industry. Colonel Rogers was indeed a pioneer in radio broadcasting in the maritimes and indeed in Canada. Ta honouring Colonel Rogers the C.A.R.T.B. honoured itself. It is interesting to note that a few days ago the governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation also approved a licence application for a television station in my riding. It will be known as CFCY-TV, and will be owned and operated by the estate of the late Colonel Rogers.
Now may I say a personal word of appreciation to my friends in this chamber who normally speak in French. Many of them have spoken in English this year so that we who are not bilingual could understand what they had to say. I deeply appreciate their courtesy. I hope that some day I may be able to converse with them in their language.
I appealed a while ago for sympathetic consideration and understanding of our mutual problems. I shall be a ready and sympathetic listener to anyone who wishes to discuss his problems. I have tried to learn something about their constituencies, and as time goes on I hope to learn more about them. Thus I shall become better acquainted with the problems of other areas as well as with those that confront my own people in Prince Edward Island, and particularly with those of Queens county.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this discussion I am not going to make any reference whatsoever to those phases of the budget speech by the Minister of Finance that had to do with fiscal policies. A great many members have already spoken on that aspect of his speech, some in condemnation and some in commendation. I want to spend what time I have on only one aspect of the minister's speech, namely his concluding remarks which can be found in Hansard at pages 2740 and 2741. I should like to recall to hon. members what he said on April 5 and what he must have thought of the important matter, because he concluded in this way:
The government intends, therefore, to appoint a royal commission with instructions to look ahead and examine carefully our future economic prospects. The sort of study we have in mind would include probable developments both in our productive capacities and in our external markets. It would include an examination of our population growth in both its regional and age distribution aspects. It would assemble information and speculate thoughtfully about the magnitude and nature of our future requirements for the great varieties of physical amenities which contribute to a steadily rising level of well-being.
He followed that up by saying:
Wise and practical policies are founded on knowledge, inspiration and courage. The Canadian

people have always demonstrated that they have Inspiration and courage. I suggest we improve our knowledge that we may not fail to take full and proper advantage of the heritage with which Providence has so richly endowed this nation.
I think the work of this royal commission will do several things. It will focus public attention, here and abroad, in a rather specific and detailed yay, on our prospects. It will gather together the considerable amount of material already in existence, but scattered in many different places, that throws light on these prospects. It will also promote and stimulate studies to fill the many gaps in essential factual material. It will sharpen our understanding of some of the problems we face, and will provide useful guides to governments and businessmen, and to leaders in all walks of life, in making plans and policies for the future.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, these concluding remarks of the Minister of Finance were the most important in his entire speech. I am very glad that at long last the government has come to a realization of the correctness of the socialist principle of looking ahead, of research and of planning. And in the words of the minister himself, we must have first of all knowledge, then vision and then the courage to act. I am glad to hear that a royal commission is to be appointed, to look ahead, to do research, to plan and make recommendations to guarantee the future well-being of all the provinces and of Canada itself. I sincerely hope that the report will not be pigeonholed and gather dust.
I can remember, sir, that it was my privilege in 1941 and 1942 to be a member of a royal commission that was called the British Columbia post-war rehabilitation council. We were told at that time by the legislature to examine the province of British Columbia, its economy, its industries, its potentialities, its needs, and to look ahead and try to come up with a plan.
It was a commission on planning appointed on a political basis. By that I mean all phases of politics were represented. As I recall it the chairman was the minister of education of British Columbia, a Liberal; another member became Speaker of the British Columbia legislature, and at the present time she is a senator from the province of British Columbia. Another member was a Conservative. He became an independent; then he became a Socred, and now he is sitting not far from here as the premier of British Columbia. It is worth while recounting that on that planning board of 1941 and 1942 I cannot remember one day or one discussion when politics ever came up as politics. A job was done and a report was made. I think it was a good one. My only regret is that it has never been acted upon. It is gathering dust somewhere in the archives of British Columbia.
I am glad to know that a federal planning commission is to be appointed, and I sincerely
The Budget-Mr. Winch hope that when the report comes down it will not gather dust, but that it will be studied and acted upon. I desire to devote my time this afternoon to only one phase of that study. It is a phase which many of you may perhaps be rather amazed to hear discussed by me, but I believe there is a study that has to be made.
I want to make as a contribution just one recommendation. It has long been my thought and my conclusion that we in Canada, and particularly in western Canada, have been missing the opportunity for a multimillion dollar industry that has always been at our doorstep. In these present days of high unemployment-according to the latest figures
640,000	are out of work in the Dominion of Canada-the governments have failed to take advantage of our resources and establish a new industry. That is something of which we should be ashamed. But, though we have failed in the past, that is no reason for failing in the future, and I should like to recommend to the Minister of Finance that in his terms of reference to the royal commission to go into research and plan the economy of Canada for the future he include research and planning to establish what I think can become one of the greatest industries in this dominion. That is the health restoring industry.
It is unfortunate that the majority of us do not appreciate good health as long as we have it, but when we lose it there is not one thing on which we are more prepared to spend money than trying to regain our health. What applies to us as individuals applies to all individuals throughout the world. I have been interested in this matter now for some 15 years. Perhaps I should explain how I became interested, because you may think that, having been an electrician or for 22 years a member of provincial and federal parliaments, I am now entering the medical field. It is for this reason. Some 15 years ago, as an electrician, I was called in to see whether I could repair certain scientific machines which were used by naturopathic physicians. These machines were imported from Europe and were unknown in North America. They used static current and galvanic current and shortwave. As a result of tinkering around and trying to fix these machines I became interested in what they were used for. That led me into a study of natural health resources.
I did not believe all I was told. Two physicians who knew something about the use of natural health measures in combination with orthodox medical restorative health measures said to me, "You bring to our attention cases of which you know personally, and for which you are certain on the advice of

The Budget-Mr. Winch medical men that nothing can be done, and let us see if anything can be done for them through the use of nature itself". I accepted that challenge, and since then I have been interested in the natural health resources of Canada. I myself have referred to the doctors people absolutely crippled with rheumatoid arthritis. One woman was under medical care and had to have nursing care 24 hours a day to move and feed her. After two years I saw that same woman getting around and looking after herself, crocheting and knitting.
I know the case of a passenger in an automobile, which skidded on the ice, went over a steep cliff and rolled over several times. One of the passengers badly tore all the ligaments of his chest. The medical advice was that he would have to be strapped for five or six weeks and be in pain most of the time. This was another good case to refer. Under what was known as the hormone peat treatment, instead of being strapped for five or six weeks before he could get up and go back to work, after 10 days he did not know that he had had an accident. I know that is true. I was the passenger in the car.
I could give you instance after instance, but I am just giving you these to illustrate how I became interested in the study. It is acknowledged throughout the world-not as a competitor with medical science but as a collaborator with medical science-that the greatest advances today are being made in the realm of natural medicine, or physical medicine. What does that mean? It means the use of the clinical nature of our hot springs, our cold springs, our radium springs, our saline muds and clays, our hormone peats, and so on. Nowhere in the world is there such an accumulation of natural healthgiving resources in the way of hormone peats, saline muds and clays, hot springs, cold springs and radium springs as we have in the Dominion of Canada. Yet we have never used them or developed their full scale of health-giving potentialities.
I know we have the radium hot springs in the national parks; we have our Harrison hot springs. They are used to attract tourists or honeymooners-a place you can go either to get on a drunk or get off a drunk- but not in the main for their health-giving purposes. Banff is closed for the greater part of the year. Our own radium hot springs are closed for the greater part of the year. Yet, when they are open, what do we have there in order to utilize the health-giving resources of the radium hot springs? You do not have to ask me; ask the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott). Unfortunately a cripple, as he is, he goes there every


year because of the help he can get there. Yet when it is open there is one physiotherapist and helper. For the majority of the year it is not open at all.
Perhaps you may think I am a visionary when I say that we have a multimillion dollar industry that we are ignoring. Let me say this. If the countries of Europe had the resources we have they would be using them. I should like to give you briefly a resume of what other people are doing with their limited resources. Mineral springs have been developed in various parts of the North American continent as well as in Europe, based on the use of hydrotherapy, physiotherapy and electrotherapy. The state of New York operates one at Saratoga Springs. It is not only health-giving, it is not only self-supporting, but it returns a revenue to the state. But it is to Europe we must go to find industries based on health.
Before the war Germany was quite frank in stating the financial value of her natural health resources. They spent enormous sums of money on research and development, and the fact that the money was not wasted is shown by this one quotation from a government report. It says this:
Many an erroneous idea of a philosophy estranged from nature had to be overcome for science and popular sentiment to combine so as to rediscover on a higher plane of knowledge the nature of medicinal springs and their functions. It is that common knowledge that makes the foundation for a sound development of Germany's medicinal springs in the interest of national business as well as in the service of mankind.
Let us go on from there and come back to North America. Just as a comparatively small illustration, on this continent we have Battle Creek which in less than 40 years has grown from a rural village to a great manufacturing centre whose products are almost entirely, directly or indirectly, built around the health centre itself.
Hon. members may be interested in learning that, according to the last figures I have, France has 186 official spas which have developed from villages of a few hundred population to great international health resorts. Germany, according to the latest figures I have-and of course they are slightly out of date now-has 212 official spas of first-class standing and many others that are not listed and, attached to these and to her universities, research institutions that have involved an outlay of millions of dollars.
Just to show the possibility of development around a spa or hot spring that has a curative value, may I say that in France there is a village which just prior to the first great war had a population of 75 to 100 people. Since the development of two small spas, one

hot and one cold, it now has a population of over 2,000 with an annual attendance of
60.000	to 80,000 visitors in search of health. There are 14 large hotels and numerous furnished villas. It requires the daily attendance of 32 doctors, with all the technicians who go with them, to take care of those who come there from all parts of the world.
Another famous spa-and I want to mention this one because its name is well known -is at Aix-les-Bains. Less than 30 years ago the population was about 2,500. Now it is 12,000. It has 45,000 visitors each year in search of health. It has four springs, two hot and two cold. They are of the sulphur type. This spa caters in particular to rheumatic and arthritic cases, and it requires 32 physicians to deal with the patients, including nine specialists in various fields. The hotels have a total accommodation of more than
4.000	rooms, in addition to pensions and large numbers of beautiful furnished villas.
I wish to mention just one more, Mr. Speaker, because you also have heard of this one but have not perhaps understood what it means. One of the largest and most fashionable spas in the world is Baden-Baden, 590 to 820 feet above sea level. The therapeutic facilities consist of the salt springs and the grape cure. There are six large sanitaria, more than 50 hotels and a large number of boarding establishments and private villas that are rented by the season. It requires 75 doctors to staff the sanitaria. Of course it must also be remembered that an average of 20 to 30 trained technicians are required for every doctor at the sanitaria in addition to cooks, gardeners and so forth.
When we recognize the fact that all the great medical authorities in the world today are turning more and more to natural health as a corollory of orthodox medicine; when we recognize the fact that a great number of people who travel from Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand to Europe are not going there for the sake of tourism but are going there in search of health; when we recognize the fact that we here in Canada have the greatest collection of natural health resources in the world, I wonder why we do not do some research and develop Canada as the land of health.
As far as my own province of British Columbia is concerned, I am convinced that within a very few years that province and western Canada generally could be known as the health mecca of the world. It requires a little bit of vision. Certainly it requires research, which I think must be done on a governmental basis. It also requires proper planning. Surely it is not too much for us to be able to conjure up in our minds what
The Budget-Mr. Winch it would mean if we made use of the God-given resources that are right at our door- even outside of health and outside of tourism -in construction, technology, new fields for medicine in this country, in maintenance and in a new market for the produce of the farmers. To me it is a "natural" going to waste.
Here on the Grand Trunk Pacific, a part of the Canadian National Railways, only 15 miles from Terrace which is now the junction point of the railway going down to Kitimat, we have the outstanding hot spring on the North American continent and, I think in the world, because it contains lithia. There are nine springs there. Only one is cribbed, but that one which is cribbed turns out
6,000	gallons of lithia water an hour. You need only go back to the writings of such famous medical men as Dr. Alexis Carrel or Lieutenant Colonel Dr. Samson of the physiotherapy branch of the United States army, to learn the use of lithia water in curing or helping people.
There it is, just 15 miles from a major centre on the Canadian National, pouring out its 6,000 gallons per hour with no use being made by the province and no use being made by the dominion of one of the great God-given, natural, health-giving resources in the entire world. If they had that in Europe-in France, in Germany, in Russia or in Switzerland-they would have a million-dollar concern right around that one spring.
I do not know the story of all Canada, but I know from my own personal knowledge of 30 hot and cold springs in the province of British Columbia. I know that we have millions of tons of what is known as hormone peat. I know of medical clays. I am sure my friend the Minister of National Defence can tell you as well as I of what the Indians can do with those clays and peats. It is almost miraculous.
There is the foundation for a new industry. I do not think people realize what we have. We have springs, hot and cold, in British Columbia. I am going to read off just what they contain, and medical men can tell you their medicinal value far better than can I. We have these right at our doorstep. These springs contain strontium sulphate, aluminum, hydrogen sulphide, calcium carbonate, calcium sulphate, magnesium carbonate, magnesium sulphate, sodium carbonate, sodium sulphate, sodium chloride, potassium chloride, lithium chloride, silica, iron and alumina. These are natural health springs known to science, and we, sir, do nothing about the matter.
3240	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Winch
I do not want to carry on beyond closing time tonight. I am convinced that we have a great natural industry at our doorstep. I am convinced that we have a multimillion dollar industry at our doorstep. I am convinced that with a little bit of attention and, to use the words of the Minister of Finance himself, research, planning and courage, we can make Canada the health mecca of the world. I am putting this forward as a constructive proposal, asking for the interest and support of hon. members.
They are not obliged to accept what I say. Let us have some research into the matter. Let us do some work on it. But I want to say this. To the best of my knowledge, throughout this country there is a great deal to offer in the realm of health not only to our own people but to the world. Doctors are more and more recognizing the need for changing altitudes and changing climates in matters of health. In our country we certainly have the changing altitudes. We certainly have the changing climates. We certainly have in almost every constituency the minerals, the springs, the fruits, the climates, the pine trees, the muds, the clays,

the peats, the bogs, the alkalis and the sunshine that can be tied in, as I say, to build a great new industry.
This is my feeling as the result of years of study, of reading the words of the world's scientists, of having cases attended to when I was faced with a challenge; and as my contribution to this debate I should like to throw out the challenge at this time that we do something about the matter, starting now.
